strengths: Well-executed conceptual contribution: the paper systematically recasts capabilities of modern SSMs (selectivity, nonlinearity, associative recall, multiscale memory, forecasting objectives) as explicit, interpretable modifications of the HiPPO framework, which is a genuinely useful analysis lens for the SSM literature.

The time-warping interpretation of Salience HiPPO (Eqs. 3-5) is elegant and technically clean: showing that scalar input-dependent scaling of the dynamics is exactly equivalent to running standard HiPPO under an invertible time reparameterization, and deriving the induced real-time history measure, makes the adaptive-memory mechanism directly visualizable.

The Multiscale HiPPO derivation (Appendix D) is technically solid: the connection between polynomial scale embeddings, Jacobi matrices, and the arcsine-law argument for why Jeffreys-style reweighting does not change the limiting timescale spectrum is a nice piece of analysis that motivates the log-timescale formulation.

Experimental reporting is unusually thorough: parameter-matched baselines, ablations over depth/capacity/data/steps for baselines (Table 3), full training details for every experiment, and multiple seeds/SEM in places.

The paper is commendably honest about limitations: it explicitly reports that HiPPO variants underperform modern SSMs on WikiText-2 (Sec. 3.6, Appendix F), that Associative Memory HiPPO fails badly on language modeling, and that the Salience-vs-Mamba comparison has confounds it cannot resolve (Appendix F.3).
The Salience-vs-Mamba delta-t analysis (F.3) is a thoughtful first step toward empirically connecting the explicit mechanism to implicit learned selectivity in a modern SSM.
weaknesses: Limited originality per component: each 'zoo member' assembles well-known ingredients — Volterra readouts are classical system identification; scalar gating of dynamics is essentially Mamba-style delta-t modulation rediscovered (the time-warp view is nice but the mechanism is close to existing selective SSMs); the OP associative memory strongly resembles kernelized fast-weight programmers / linear-attention key-value memories; multiscale SSM banks exist (e.g., H3-adjacent multiscale work). The contribution is a unification and interpretability framework more than new methods, which limits significance.

Empirical evidence is restricted to synthetic tasks designed by the authors to align with each explicit mechanism, creating a circularity risk: a mechanism tailored to a task naturally wins on that task. The one real-data evaluation (WikiText-2, ~25k parameters) shows the variants underperform even a comparable LSTM, and Associative Memory HiPPO catastrophically fails, so practical value beyond interpretability is not demonstrated.

The headline comparisons are on very small models (~25k params, single layer) and short synthetic episodes (e.g., AR task with T=12), which weakens claims that linear recurrence 'cannot bind arbitrary key-value pairs' — modern associative-recall results at larger scale do not obviously support this general conclusion.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link is effectively blank in the manuscript ('Code available at' with no URL), and several results rely on author-designed tasks whose exact generative procedures span multiple appendix sections, making independent verification harder.

Depth per extension is shallow; each of the five variants gets roughly one synthetic experiment, and no variant is stress-tested beyond its showcase setting. The 'zoo' framing makes the paper feel like a collection of modest extensions rather than a single substantive advance.

Some analyses lack rigor: the kernel-reconstruction interpretation of learned quadratic readouts (Fig. 1) is qualitative; the claim that Salience HiPPO's scalar gating is 'simpler than entrywise gating' yet achieves 100% is not disentangled from task design or the extra state-dependence of g(t).
Minor presentation issues: several typos ('an low-rank map', '¿60%', '+' at end of a sentence in App. D), and Figure 2 readability could be improved.

strengths: The paper is mathematically careful and well-organized: each extension is derived from first principles within the HiPPO/OP framework, and the appendices provide substantial derivational detail (e.g., Favard's theorem, the reproducing-kernel write update, the reduced-rank regression connection).

The time-warping interpretation of Salience HiPPO (Eqs. 3-5) is genuinely elegant: it reduces input-dependent gating to an invertible reparameterization of the time axis and makes the induced real-time history measure explicit, which is a real analytical contribution.

The honest treatment of trade-offs is commendable: the paper explicitly reports that its variants underperform modern SSMs on WikiText-2 and frames the work as prioritizing interpretability over performance, rather than overclaiming.

The diagnostic visualizations (induced history measures, learned write/read addresses, OP memory before/after writes, objective-induced history kernels) directly support the central interpretability claim, and the F.3 analysis relating scalar salience to Mamba's vector-valued Δt is a thoughtful probe.

The Jeffreys-prior discussion (Appendix D.2) using the arcsine-law result of Kuijlaars & Van Assche to show that reweighting the scale measure does not change the limiting spectrum is a nice piece of analysis that motivates the log-timescale variant.
Code availability and detailed experimental protocols (optimizers, learning rates, ZOH discretization, parameter counts) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited per-extension novelty. Salience HiPPO (Eq. 2) is a scalar multiplicative rescaling of the integration rate, which is essentially a scalar version of input-dependent Δt as in Mamba and input-dependent discretization used in prior continuous-time RNN work (e.g., Liquid time-constant networks, Liquid-S4); the paper's own time-warping analysis confirms it is a reparameterized standard HiPPO. Multiscale HiPPO is admitted in Appendix D.4 to 'not introduce fundamentally richer dynamics than a bank of independent HiPPO systems.' Volterra polynomial readouts are classical system identification applied on top of a HiPPO state.

The associative memory extension is presented as if associative/key-value memory in linear recurrent models were an open problem, but the paper does not engage with the substantial fast-weights and linear-attention literature (fast weight programmers, DeltaNet, linear attention/outer-product KV memories, TTT, Hopfield-style memories) where explicitly stored key-value associations are standard. This omission weakens the originality framing considerably.

The evaluation has a circularity problem: each variant is tested on a bespoke synthetic task seemingly designed to match that variant's inductive bias (a task that is exactly second-order Volterra for Volterra HiPPO; selective copying for Salience; a tiny T=12 associative recall task for the associative memory variant). Standard benchmarks from the SSM associative-recall literature (e.g., MQAR as in Zoology/Based) are not used, making cross-work comparison impossible and inflating the apparent advantage of 'task-aligned explicit structure.'

Baseline comparisons may be undertuned: all models are trained for only 4,000 gradient steps at ~25k parameters, and broad claims are then drawn (e.g., 'linear recurrence with limited nonlinearity cannot bind arbitrary key-value pairs' based on S4D failing at two depths). Table 3 itself shows 2-layer transformers reach ~99%, so the task is solvable by standard models; the marginal value of the explicit mechanism over adequately scaled baselines is not firmly established.

Real-data results are weak and, for one variant, catastrophically so (Associative Memory HiPPO at 20.41 PPL on WikiText-2 versus 4.65-5.75 for baselines). The paper frames this honestly, but it means the 'zoo' has no demonstrated utility beyond its own synthetic tasks, limiting significance for a main-track audience.

Significance is niche: the discussion concludes that practitioners should use Mamba/S4D when performance matters and use the zoo only when transparency is essential, without demonstrating a concrete application (scientific modeling, streaming system identification beyond a single benchmark system) where the interpretability yields actionable insight.

Missing comparisons to directly relevant adaptive-timescale and multiscale prior work (e.g., Liquid-S4, input-dependent Δt variants, multiscale SSMs of Goel et al. beyond a passing citation), which would sharpen the delta over prior art.

Minor presentation defects suggest insufficient polish: a '¿60%' encoding artifact on page 19, a stray '+' after 'Section 3.4' on page 20, and the code footnote on page 2 appears to lack an actual URL.
